metadata.title: GATmath and GATLc: Comprehensive benchmarks for evaluating Arabic large language models

abstract: The evolution of Large Language Models (LLMs) has significantly advanced artificial intelligence, driving innovation across various applications. Their continued development relies on a deep understanding of their capabilities and limitations. This is achieved primarily through rigorous evaluation based on diverse datasets. However, assessing state-of-the-art models in Arabic remains a formidable challenge due to the scarcity of comprehensive benchmarks. The absence of robust evaluation tools hinders the progress and refinement of Arabic LLMs and limits their potential applications and effectiveness in real-world scenarios. In response, we introduce the GATmath (7k questions) and GATLc (9k questions), two Arabic, large-scale, and multitask reasoning and language understanding benchmarks. Derived from the General Aptitude Test (GAT) examination, each dataset covers multiple categories, demanding skills in reasoning, semantic analysis, language comprehension, and mathematical problem-solving. To the best of our knowledge, our dataset is the first comprehensive and large-scale reasoning dataset specifically tailored to the Arabic language. We conducted a comprehensive evaluation and analysis of seven prominent LLMs on our datasets. Remarkably, even the highest-performing model attained a mere 66.9% and 64.3% accuracy, underscoring the considerable challenge posed by our datasets. This outcome illustrates the intricate nature of the tasks within our datasets and highlights the substantial room for improvement in the realm of Arabic language model development.

key_findings.claim: Qwen2-72B-Instruct achieves the highest performance among all evaluated models on GATmath (66.9% average accuracy) and GATLc (64.3% average accuracy), yet still falls well below human-level performance.
key_findings.context: 5-shot in-context learning evaluation across 7 Arabic LLMs on two novel Arabic benchmarks

key_findings.claim: Model size positively correlates with benchmark performance across both GATmath and GATLc datasets, with 70B+ parameter models consistently outperforming 13B models.
key_findings.quantitative_result: Qwen2-72B: 66.9% vs jais-13b: 26.2% on GATmath; Qwen2-72B: 64.3% vs jais-13b: 32.3% on GATLc
key_findings.context: Consistent pattern observed across all 7 models evaluated

key_findings.claim: Strong performance on English-language mathematical benchmarks does not transfer to Arabic mathematical reasoning; Llama3-70b-instruct scored 93% on GSM8K but only 46.8% on GATmath.
key_findings.quantitative_result: Llama3-70b: GSM8K 93% vs GATmath 46.8%; Qwen2-72B: GSM8K 91.1% vs GATmath 66.9%
key_findings.context: Cross-lingual comparison of model performance on English vs Arabic math benchmarks

key_findings.claim: Strong performance on English language comprehension benchmarks does not transfer to Arabic language understanding; Llama3-70b-instruct scored 87.5% on FEval but only 49.9% on GATLc.
key_findings.quantitative_result: Llama3-70b: FEval 87.5%, MMLU 86%, ARC Challenge 94.8% vs GATLc 49.9%
key_findings.context: Cross-lingual performance gap observed consistently across all tested models

key_findings.claim: The Comparisons task in GATmath is the most challenging category for all models, including the top performer Qwen2-72B-Instruct which achieves only 58.5%, suggesting models struggle with abstract relational reasoning in Arabic.
key_findings.quantitative_result: Qwen2-72B Comparisons: 58.5% (lowest task score for top model on GATmath)
key_findings.context: Task-specific analysis within the GATmath benchmark

key_findings.claim: Contextual Error and Verbal Analogy tasks in GATLc are the most challenging categories, with even top models struggling to exceed 60% accuracy, indicating difficulties with contextual semantic understanding in Arabic.
key_findings.quantitative_result: Qwen2-72B Contextual Error: 58.5%; Analogy: 59.0%; jais-30b Contextual Error: 27.3%
key_findings.context: Task-specific analysis within the GATLc benchmark across 5 task types

key_findings.claim: ALLaM-70B demonstrates domain-specific specialization, performing better on GATLc (62.7%) than GATmath (57.4%), suggesting its training is better aligned with linguistic analysis than mathematical reasoning.
key_findings.context: Cross-dataset comparison revealing domain-specific model strengths

key_findings.claim: Model rankings can reverse across domains: Llama3-70b-instruct outperforms ALLaM-13B on GATmath (46.8% vs 41.7%) but is outperformed by ALLaM-13B on GATLc (49.9% vs 52.8%), indicating domain-specific capabilities.
key_findings.quantitative_result: GATmath: Llama3-70b 46.8% > ALLaM-13B 41.7%; GATLc: ALLaM-13B 52.8% > Llama3-70b 49.9%
key_findings.context: Comparative analysis between GATmath and GATLc results

key_findings.claim: jais-13b-chat and AceGPT-13B-chat achieve the lowest performance among evaluated models, both averaging 26.2% on GATmath, only marginally above the random baseline of 25% for 4-choice questions.
key_findings.context: Evaluation of Arabic-focused smaller models against the GATmath benchmark

key_findings.claim: GATmath and GATLc present a more challenging and comprehensive Arabic benchmark than prior work, with 7,016 and 9,036 questions respectively, compared to the 924-question Alkaoud dataset and 412 Arabic math questions in ArabicMMLU.
key_findings.quantitative_result: GATmath: 7,016 questions; GATLc: 9,036 questions; total: 16,052 questions
key_findings.context: Comparison with prior Arabic NLP benchmark datasets

key_findings.claim: GATmath uniquely represents all numbers, variables, and mathematical symbols in Arabic characters, distinguishing it from prior Arabic math datasets like ArMATH where numbers and variables are in English.
key_findings.context: Differentiating characteristic versus ArMATH and ArabicMMLU math subset

key_findings.claim: Qwen2-72B-Instruct excels at sentence completion in GATLc (77.4%), demonstrating relatively strong proficiency in Arabic grammatical accuracy and logical coherence compared to other task types.
key_findings.quantitative_result: Sentence Completion: 77.4% (highest task-specific score for any model on GATLc)
key_findings.context: Task-level analysis of top-performing model on GATLc

llm_extraction.methods_summary: Two large-scale Arabic benchmark datasets (GATmath and GATLc) were constructed from Saudi Arabia's General Aptitude Test (GAT) exam. Questions were manually transcribed from image-based PDFs by 10 freelancers (5 per dataset) recruited from Upwork and Bahr platforms, following a standardized guide. Transcribed data were reviewed by 2 expert freelancers (one mathematics specialist, one linguistics specialist) in batches of 300 questions. After automated duplicate removal, the final datasets comprised 7,016 GATmath questions (4 task types: Algebra, Problem Solving, Geometry, Comparisons) and 9,036 GATLc questions (5 task types: Verbal Analogy, Sentence Completion, Contextual Error, Semantic Association and Disparity, Reading Comprehension). Seven Arabic LLMs were evaluated using 5-shot in-context learning (ICL) via the lm-evaluation-harness framework: jais-13b-chat, jais-30b-chat, AceGPT-13B-chat, LLaMA3-70b-instruct, ALLaM-13B, ALLaM-SFT-70B, and Qwen2-72B-Instruct. Evaluation metric was accuracy (percentage of correct multiple-choice answers). Prompts replicated those from the official GAT examination to minimize prompt bias. Cross-lingual comparisons were made against published scores on English benchmarks (GSM8K, MGSM, MMLU, FEval, ARC Challenge, HellaSwag, WinoGrande).
llm_extraction.limitations: Image-based geometry questions (containing charts and figures) were excluded from GATmath, reducing ecological validity for the geometry subset. No formal error analysis was conducted to identify specific error types or patterns. The benchmark is limited to multiple-choice questions (4 options), which does not capture open-ended generation capabilities. Only 7 models were evaluated, and several recent state-of-the-art models (e.g., GPT-4, Claude) were not included. The dataset construction relied on freelancer transcription, which may introduce transcription errors despite quality control measures. The study does not evaluate zero-shot performance, limiting understanding of how prompting strategy affects results. Image-based questions, which constitute a significant portion of the original GAT exam, are not covered, necessitating future vision-LLM evaluation.

relationships.description: GATLc extends Alkaoud's GAT verbal dataset by adding the Semantic Association and Disparity task type (absent from Alkaoud), expanding from 924 to 9,036 questions, and covering the full bipartite structure of the GAT exam including the mathematical section.

GATmath extends ArMATH by covering high school-level (not elementary) mathematics with multiple variables, representing all numbers and symbols in Arabic characters (vs English in ArMATH), and providing a larger dataset (7,016 vs ~6,000 questions).
GATmath provides a more comprehensive Arabic math benchmark than the 412 elementary-level English-number math questions in ArabicMMLU, covering higher-level GAT exam mathematics entirely in Arabic.

GATmath and GATLc extend the Arabic subset of EXAMS (562 questions) with a much larger dataset requiring complex skills such as semantic analysis, reasoning, and mathematical problem solving, unlike EXAMS Arabic which tests only general knowledge recall.

GATLc and GATmath mirror the MMLU paradigm for Arabic language evaluation, analogous to how ArabicMMLU mirrors MMLU, but specifically grounded in the culturally and linguistically authentic Saudi GAT examination framework.

GATmath demonstrates that Arabic mathematical reasoning benchmarks reveal substantial performance gaps compared to English benchmarks like GSM8K, revealing cross-lingual generalization failures not captured by English-only evaluation.

methodology_details.approach: Benchmark dataset construction from human exam questions (Saudi Arabia GAT) via manual transcription by freelancers, expert revision, automated deduplication, and evaluation of 7 Arabic LLMs using 5-shot in-context learning via lm-evaluation-harness framework.
datasets: GATmath (7,016 questions: Algebra, Problem Solving, Geometry, Comparisons)
GATLc (9,036 questions: Verbal Analogy, Sentence Completion, Contextual Error, Semantic Association and Disparity, Reading Comprehension)
metrics: Accuracy (percentage of correct multiple-choice answers per task and overall)
methodology_details.reproducibility_notes: Datasets formatted as human-readable JSON with proper indentation. Evaluation conducted using the open-source lm-evaluation-harness framework, enabling community reproducibility. Prompts standardized to match official GAT examination prompts. 5-shot examples curated from each task type.

domain_specific_fields.benchmark: GATmath (7,016 questions, 4 tasks) and GATLc (9,036 questions, 5 tasks), derived from Saudi Arabia's General Aptitude Test (GAT); total 16,052 questions across 9 categories
domain_specific_fields.metrics: Accuracy (% correct on 4-option multiple-choice questions), evaluated per task and overall average; 5-shot in-context learning setting
domain_specific_fields.model_architecture: Evaluated models: jais-13b-chat, jais-30b-chat (73B token Arabic corpus), AceGPT-13B-chat (RLHF-enhanced), LLaMA3-70b-instruct (Meta AI), ALLaM-13B, ALLaM-SFT-70B (LLaMA-derived, Arabic cultural alignment), Qwen2-72B-Instruct (0.5B–72B series, instruction-tuned); architectures include encoder-only (AraBERT family), encoder-decoder (AraT5), and decoder-only models
domain_specific_fields.dataset: Sourced from publicly available GAT preparation platforms via image-based PDFs; manually transcribed by 10 Upwork/Bahr freelancers; revised by 2 domain experts; image-based geometry questions excluded; all mathematical symbols and numbers in GATmath represented in Arabic characters; JSON format with human-readable indentation
